stem: An eight-year-old child presents for evaluation of ongoing concerns for inability to sit still, distractibility, and poor academic achievement. Sleep problems and loud snoring are reported. Which condition is most likely to co-occur with the child's presenting disorder?
explanation_text: Inattention, hyperactivity, and loud snoring point to ADHD with likely obstructive sleep apnea. OSA's most characteristic pediatric psychiatric/medical comorbidity among these choices is nocturnal enuresis. Seizures, migraine, hearing loss, and autoimmunity are not the typical pairing. Teaching point: Snoring ADHD kid → ask about bedwetting; treat the airway.
clinical_application: An 8-year-old referred for ADHD snores loudly and wets the bed most nights. The resident does not start a stimulant until sleep is addressed, and specifically asks about enuresis — OSA's frequent roommate. A sleep study and ENT referral may do more for attention than another dose increase. Seizures and migraine are not the typical pairing. Bottom line: Snoring plus inattention → ask about bedwetting and the airway.
video_query: Psychopathology Enuresis child psychiatry

stem: Guided play, a child-led activity in which trusted adults craft an environment to enhance learning, is most closely aligned with which cognitive developmental concepts?
explanation_text: Guided play is an adult arranging the environment so the child can do with help what they cannot yet do alone — Vygotsky's zone of proximal development. Decentration and conservation are Piagetian concrete-operational achievements. Reciprocal determinism is Bandura. Assimilation/accommodation is Piaget's adaptation, not the scaffolding idea. Teaching point: Adult-crafted, child-led play = ZPD.
clinical_application: A preschool teacher has set out blocks and a story prompt, then steps back while a 4-year-old builds 'the zoo' with just enough help to keep going. The resident recognizes Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, not Piagetian conservation or Bandura. They coach parents to arrange the room so the child can do with help what they cannot yet do alone. Bottom line: Adult-crafted, child-led play is the zone of proximal development.
video_query: Development Zone of proximal development child psychiatry

stem: A 13-year-old patient with autism and developmental delays is admitted to the medical hospital with a diagnosis of catatonia. After one week of high-dose benzodiazepine therapy, there is minimal improvement. Which of the following is the best treatment option to utilize next?

options.text: Addition of a neuroleptic such as olanzapine
Addition of an antiepileptic such as valproic acid

explanation_text: Catatonia that fails high-dose benzodiazepines next goes to ECT, including in autistic and developmentally delayed youth. Adding a neuroleptic can worsen catatonia (or NMS). rTMS and valproate are not first-line rescue. Staying the course after a failed week is not appropriate. Teaching point: Benzo-refractory catatonia → ECT, not an antipsychotic.
clinical_application: A 13-year-old with autism is admitted for catatonia. High-dose lorazepam for a week has barely moved the Bush-Francis score. The resident pages ECT, not olanzapine. Adding a neuroleptic can worsen catatonia. They prepare the family for a time-sensitive conversation and hold off on 'give it another week.' Bottom line: Benzodiazepine-refractory catatonia goes to ECT, including in autistic youth.

stem: Which of the following mood stabilizers is FDA-approved for acute mania and maintenance of bipolar disorder in youth greater than 12 years of age?
explanation_text: Lithium is FDA-approved for acute mania and maintenance in youth ≥12. Divalproex, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, and carbamazepine are used off-label or for other indications; none share that exact pediatric bipolar approval. Teaching point: Lithium is the age-12+ FDA mood stabilizer for mania and maintenance.
clinical_application: A 14-year-old is admitted for mania. The team wants an FDA-backed mood stabilizer for both the acute episode and maintenance. The resident chooses lithium — approved for youth 12 and older — rather than defaulting to valproate or lamotrigine. Labs, pregnancy counseling, and thyroid/renal monitoring are set up before the first dose. Bottom line: Lithium is the age-12+ FDA mood stabilizer for acute mania and maintenance.

stem: A school-aged child presents to clinic with their parents for frequently losing their temper at home, pranking their classmates at school, blaming others for their mistakes, and getting into arguments with their teacher over the past six months. Which is the most common comorbid condition found in children with this disorder?
explanation_text: Temper loss, arguing with adults, blaming, and annoying others for ≥6 months is ODD. The most common comorbidity is ADHD (well over half of clinic ODD). Tourette, SUD, SAD, and OCD co-occur less often. Teaching point: ODD → look for ADHD first.
clinical_application: Clinic: six months of arguing, blaming, and annoying teachers. The resident diagnoses ODD and then screens ADHD before anything else. Most clinic ODD travels with ADHD; Tourette, OCD, and SAD are less common companions. The treatment plan pairs parent management with an ADHD workup rather than ODD-only therapy. Bottom line: New ODD → look for ADHD first.

stem: A 12-year-old presents with a history of bilateral frontal headaches that occur twice a month, associated with photophobia and vomiting. Which of the following is the best pharmacological intervention to prevent future headaches?
explanation_text: Twice-monthly migraines with photophobia and vomiting warrant prevention. Propranolol is a first-line pediatric migraine preventive. Ibuprofen, sumatriptan, ergotamine, and prochlorperazine are abortive (or antiemetic) agents, not preventives. Teaching point: Pediatric migraine prevention = propranolol (or a TCA/topiramate); triptans treat the attack.
clinical_application: A 12-year-old has twice-monthly frontal headaches with photophobia and vomiting. Ibuprofen helps an attack but they keep coming. The resident starts propranolol for prevention and keeps triptans or antiemetics for the acute episode. They check asthma and resting pulse before writing the beta-blocker. Bottom line: Pediatric migraine prevention is propranolol (or a TCA/topiramate), not a daily triptan.

stem: A child has frequent mispronunciations, such as "bofroom" for "bathroom." This language error is most consistent with which of the disorders below?
explanation_text: Substituting sounds ('bofroom' for 'bathroom') is a speech-sound (articulation/phonological) error. Receptive/expressive language disorders affect meaning and grammar, fluency is stuttering, and social-pragmatic disorder is use of language in context. Teaching point: Wrong sounds, intact meaning = speech-sound disorder.
clinical_application: A kindergarten teacher reports 'bofroom' for bathroom and 'pasgetti' for spaghetti. Meaning and grammar are fine; no stutter. The resident labels a speech-sound disorder and refers to speech therapy, not a language or pragmatic workup. Parents leave knowing this is about sounds, not intelligence. Bottom line: Wrong sounds with intact meaning is a speech-sound disorder.

stem: The Positive Action Program is a school-based program that teaches self-management skills and strategies to increase the use of positive social behavior among all elementary and middle school students, without regard to specific risk factors. This program is an example of which type of preventive intervention?
explanation_text: A program delivered to all students regardless of risk is universal (primary) prevention. Selective targets a risk group; indicated/tertiary targets already-symptomatic youth; secondary is early detection. Teaching point: Whole-school, no risk screen = universal prevention.
clinical_application: The school asks the consultant to review Positive Action, taught to every student with no risk screen. The resident files it as universal prevention and contrasts it with selective (a risk group) and indicated (already symptomatic) programs. Budget conversations get clearer once the tier is named. Bottom line: A whole-school program with no risk filter is universal prevention.

stem: Which of the following health promotion strategies has the most evidence for preventing mental illness in children?
explanation_text: The prevention intervention with the strongest child mental-health evidence is treating parental psychiatric illness. Exercise, music, mindfulness, and micronutrients have weaker or mixed preventive data. Teaching point: Treat the parent's illness to prevent the child's.
clinical_application: A well-child visit family wants the 'best thing to prevent mental illness' — yoga, violin, vitamins, or treating mom's untreated depression. The resident is honest: treating parental psychopathology has the strongest child-prevention evidence. They offer mom a same-week intake and keep the lifestyle ideas as extras, not the main plan. Bottom line: Treat the parent's illness to prevent the child's.

stem: In the early stages of human brain development, which structure gives rise to the cerebral cortex?
explanation_text: The telencephalon (prosencephalic vesicle) gives rise to the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and basal ganglia. Diencephalon → thalamus/hypothalamus; mesencephalon → midbrain; rhombencephalon/myelencephalon → hindbrain/medulla. Teaching point: Cortex comes from telencephalon.
clinical_application: On pediatric neurology rounds someone asks which embryonic vesicle becomes cortex. The resident answers telencephalon and places diencephalon with thalamus, mesencephalon with midbrain. A quick sketch on the board keeps the consult team from mixing up the vesicles on the next board question — and the next MRI read. Bottom line: Cerebral cortex comes from telencephalon.

stem: Which of the following types of experimental studies is specifically designed to examine how well a treatment works under real-world conditions?
explanation_text: Effectiveness trials test how a treatment works in real-world, usual-care conditions. Efficacy trials test it under ideal, tightly controlled conditions. Naturalistic, crossover, and meta-analysis are designs, not that distinction. Teaching point: Efficacy = can it work; effectiveness = does it work out there.
clinical_application: Journal club: a community clinic wants to know if a parenting program 'works out there,' not just in a university lab. The resident asks whether the trial is effectiveness (usual-care, real-world) or efficacy (ideal, tightly selected). They stop the group from treating those words as synonyms. Bottom line: Efficacy asks if it can work; effectiveness asks if it does work in the wild.
video_query: Research Methods Effectiveness child psychiatry

stem: A five-year-old child presents with a one-year history of worsening difficulty climbing stairs and running. Electromyography demonstrates a pattern of low amplitude motor action potentials of short duration. Which of the following diagnoses is most characteristic of these findings?
explanation_text: Progressive proximal weakness in a preschooler plus myopathic EMG (low-amplitude, short-duration MUAP) is Duchenne muscular dystrophy. MG is fatigable with decrement on repetitive stim. MS is central and rare at 5. Polio is neuropathic (large-amplitude MUAPs). LGS is an epilepsy syndrome. Teaching point: Toddler/preschool boy, stairs, myopathic EMG = DMD.
clinical_application: A 5-year-old boy has a year of worsening stair-climbing and running. EMG shows low-amplitude, short-duration motor-unit potentials. The resident thinks Duchenne, not MG, MS, or polio, and involves neuromuscular clinic and genetics. CK and a dystrophin workup follow; they do not start with an epilepsy protocol. Bottom line: Preschool proximal weakness plus a myopathic EMG is Duchenne until proven otherwise.
video_query: Neuroscience Duchenne muscular dystrophy child psychiatry

stem: Which of the following symptoms is most likely to distinguish children with early onset schizophrenia from those with non-psychotic behavioral or emotional disorders?
explanation_text: Hallucinations, irritability, language delay, and withdrawal occur in many non-psychotic childhood disorders (anxiety, trauma, ASD, depression). Formal thought disorder — loose associations — more specifically marks early-onset schizophrenia. Teaching point: Looseness of associations separates EOS from look-alike behavioral disorders.
clinical_application: An 11-year-old is withdrawn, irritable, and sometimes 'hears a whisper.' The team is split between early schizophrenia and severe anxiety. The resident listens for loose associations — formal thought disorder — which more specifically marks early-onset schizophrenia. Hallucinations and withdrawal occur in many non-psychotic childhood disorders. Bottom line: Looseness of associations helps separate early-onset schizophrenia from look-alike behavioral disorders.
video_query: Psychopathology Loose associations child psychiatry

stem: During a Parent-Child Interaction Therapy (PCIT) session, a parent is coached to play "picnic" with their child. The child says, "Yum, ice cream!" and pretends to lick a plastic scoop of ice cream. In response, the parent says, "You think the ice cream is yummy." Which of the following PCIT child-directed interaction skills is the child's parent exhibiting?
explanation_text: Repeating the child's meaning ('You think the ice cream is yummy') is PRIDE Reflection. Praise would value the act, imitation would do the same action, behavioral description would narrate the behavior, enjoyment is the 'E' affect. Teaching point: PCIT reflection = say back the child's words/meaning.
clinical_application: Behind the one-way mirror, a parent in PCIT says, 'You think the ice cream is yummy,' after the child pretends to lick a scoop. The coach marks Reflection, not Praise, Imitation, or Behavioral Description. The parent is learning to say the child's meaning back, not to evaluate or copy the play. Bottom line: PCIT reflection is repeating the child's words or meaning.

stem: A patient presents to clinic, accompanied by parents, with reports of recent personality changes, tremors, and aggression. The parents also report that a relative had a similar presentation that eventually led to a liver transplant. Which disorder is the patient most likely suffering from?
explanation_text: Personality change, tremor, aggression, plus a relative who needed a liver transplant is Wilson disease (ATP7B, copper, Kayser–Fleischer, low ceruloplasmin). Niemann–Pick is storage/hepatosplenomegaly; Huntington is typically adult CAG; the ataxias and idiopathic cirrhosis lack this neuropsychiatric + transplant pedigree. Teaching point: New neuropsych + liver family history = Wilson.
clinical_application: A teen arrives with new personality change, tremor, and aggression. An uncle needed a liver transplant after a similar illness. The resident orders ceruloplasmin and slit-lamp exam for Wilson disease before assuming primary psychosis. Niemann–Pick and Huntington do not fit this age-plus-liver pedigree. Bottom line: New neuropsych plus a liver-transplant relative is Wilson until cleared.

stem: The parent of a patient reviews medical records and strongly disagrees with the diagnosis and asks the physician to change the diagnosis. How should the physician manage the documentation?

options.text: Emphasize the accuracy of the diagnosis.
Explicitly acknowledge the difference of opinion on the diagnosis.
Write a biopsychosocial formulation without any mention of the diagnosis.
Use a euphemism for the diagnosis that professionals will recognize.
Refer to International Classification of Disease codes rather than DSM-5 labels.

answer_text: Explicitly acknowledge the difference of opinion on the diagnosis.
answer_raw: B. Explicitly acknowledge the difference of opinion on the diagnosis.
explanation_text: Patients/parents may disagree with a diagnosis; the record should document that disagreement rather than erase, euphemize, or code-hide the clinical impression. Emphasizing 'I am right' is adversarial; omitting the diagnosis is inaccurate. Teaching point: Keep the diagnosis and explicitly note the family's dissent.
clinical_application: A father reads the note, disagrees with the ADHD diagnosis, and asks that it be deleted. The resident keeps the clinical impression and adds a sentence that the family disagrees. They do not euphemize, code-hide, or write a formulation with no diagnosis. Bottom line: Keep the diagnosis and explicitly document the family's dissent.

stem: A study is comparing the electroencephalogram (EEG) data between two groups of individuals. From each EEG node, the between-group difference of signal amplitudes over time was examined. Running statistical tests for every time point will increase the likelihood of a type I error. Which is the best solution for this problem?

options.text: Show evidence of sufficient statistical power.

explanation_text: Testing every EEG time point inflates type I error (false positives). The direct fix is a multiple-comparison correction (Bonferroni, FDR, cluster-based permutation). Hierarchical/mixed models and nonparametric tests address other problems; power speaks to type II error. Teaching point: Many tests → correct for multiple comparisons.
clinical_application: A research meeting: the fellow wants to t-test every EEG time point between groups. The resident stops the plan — that is a type I error factory — and asks for a multiple-comparison correction or a cluster test. Power calculations address misses, not false positives. Bottom line: Many tests require a multiple-comparisons correction.
video_query: Research Methods Implement multiple comparison analyses. child psychiatry

stem: During a neurological exam, a child is asked to stand up, close their eyes, and stretch out their arms. The examiner then lightly pushes the child to see if they can remain standing. This test is designed to assess:
explanation_text: Eyes-closed stance with a light push is a proprioceptive / joint-position-sense (Romberg-like) challenge. It is not a test of praxis, executive function, isolated core strength, or simple command-following. Teaching point: Eyes closed + perturbation = joint position sense.
clinical_application: On the ward the resident asks a child to stand, close their eyes, and hold their arms out, then gives a light push. They are testing joint-position sense, not core strength or following commands. A sway with eyes closed that steadies with eyes open points to proprioception. Bottom line: Eyes-closed stance plus a light push assesses joint-position sense.
video_query: Assessment joint position sense. child psychiatry

stem: A researcher wants to measure the amygdalar activity in patients with conduct disorder. Which of the following imaging studies would be best to use?
explanation_text: Amygdalar activity (function, not structure) is measured with fMRI. CT is structure. DTI is white-matter tracts. PET/SPECT can measure activity but are more invasive, lower resolution, and not first choice for this question. Teaching point: Functional amygdala question → fMRI.
clinical_application: A protocol wants to measure amygdala activity in youth with conduct disorder. The resident picks fMRI, not CT, DTI, or a nuclear study as first choice. Structure and tracts will not answer an activity question. Bottom line: Functional amygdala questions are fMRI questions.
video_query: Neuroscience Functional magnetic resonance imaging child psychiatry

stem: A researcher wants to search for genetic variants that might contribute to early-onset psychosis and collaborates with other researchers to collect DNA samples from a large group of children. Genotypes are determined on thousands of single nucleotide polymorphisms for each sample, and data are analyzed to find loci that are affected at a significant frequency in affected children compared to children without psychosis. This approach is best described as which of the following techniques?
explanation_text: Genotyping thousands of SNPs across many cases vs controls to find frequency differences is a GWAS. Fine mapping narrows a known locus; linkage uses pedigrees; WES reads coding sequence; FISH sees large cytogenetic targets. Teaching point: Lots of SNPs × case–control = GWAS.
clinical_application: A multi-site child-psychosis genetics meeting is genotyping thousands of SNPs in cases versus controls. The resident names it a GWAS, not WES, linkage, or FISH. They help the team explain to families that this finds common frequency differences, not a single-gene diagnosis. Bottom line: Lots of SNPs times case–control is a GWAS.
video_query: Research Methods Genome-wide association study child psychiatry

stem: Which of the following best describes the use of pedigree analysis?

options.text: Detecting low penetrance variants in homogeneous populations
Detecting common disease variants in heterogeneous populations
Mapping loci that contribute to variation in continuously varying traits
Examining allele frequencies in transmitted and non-transmitted chromosomes in families
Identifying chromosomal regions shared by siblings concordant for a disease

answer_text: Mapping loci that contribute to variation in continuously varying traits
answer_raw: C. Mapping loci that contribute to variation in continuously varying traits
explanation_text: Pedigree-based analyses (including quantitative-trait linkage) are used to map loci that contribute to continuously varying familial traits. Common-variant detection in mixed populations is GWAS; TDT looks at transmitted vs non-transmitted alleles; affected-sib-pair sharing is nonparametric linkage. Teaching point: Pedigrees map familial — including quantitative — trait loci.
clinical_application: In genetics clinic a fellow asks what pedigree analysis is actually for. The resident describes mapping familial — including quantitative — trait loci through family structure, not hunting common variants in mixed populations (that is GWAS). They sketch a three-generation tree on the whiteboard to show the method. Bottom line: Pedigrees map familial, including quantitative, trait loci.

stem: A psychiatrist explains the purpose of the fight-or-flight system to an adolescent with an anxiety disorder. The psychiatrist is giving which of the following explanations of anxiety?
explanation_text: Explaining fight-or-flight as a useful survival system is an adaptive (functional) model of anxiety. Descriptive names the syndrome, mechanistic names circuits/transmitters, ontogenetic names development, environmental names triggers. Teaching point: 'Your alarm system is trying to keep you safe' = adaptive formulation.
clinical_application: A teen with panic says their body is 'broken.' The resident explains fight-or-flight as a useful alarm that is misfiring. That is an adaptive formulation, not a neurotransmitter lecture or a list of DSM criteria. The teen leaves with a less catastrophic story about their own physiology. Bottom line: 'Your alarm is trying to keep you safe' is an adaptive model of anxiety.
video_query: Psychotherapy Adaptive child psychiatry

stem: Which is the best way for a parent to implement time out for a ten-year-old child?

options.text: Always end after a predetermined amount of time.
Place the child in the bedroom to help distract them.
Use light spanking if the child is unwilling to stay in time out.
Use for only one or two behaviors at a time.
Actively remind the child why the time out is occurring.

answer_text: Use for only one or two behaviors at a time.
answer_raw: D. Use for only one or two behaviors at a time.
explanation_text: Time-out works when it is used for one or two target behaviors, is boring (not the bedroom's toys), is not paired with spanking, and is not narrated throughout. A fixed clock ending regardless of calm can reward the tantrum; the child should be calm before release. Teaching point: Time-out: few target behaviors, dull place, no spank, no running commentary.
clinical_application: Parents want a timeout script for a 10-year-old. The resident picks one or two target behaviors, a dull spot (not the toy-filled bedroom), no spanking, and no running commentary. A kitchen timer that ends whether or not the child is calm can reward the tantrum. They role-play one timeout in the office so the parents feel the difference. Bottom line: Timeout works when it is brief, boring, and reserved for one or two behaviors.
video_query: Psychotherapy Use for only one or two behaviors at a time. child psychiatry

stem: During the moments after a car accident, an adolescent describes feeling calm, losing sense of time, and floating above the car watching the events occur. Which of the following terms best describes this symptom?
explanation_text: Watching oneself from above, time distortion, and odd calm during trauma is depersonalization (detachment from self). Derealization is detachment from the world; illusion/hallucination are perceptual errors; fugue is amnestic wandering. Teaching point: Out-of-body during a crash = depersonalization.
clinical_application: After a crash, a teen says they felt calm, lost time, and watched themselves from above the car. The resident names depersonalization, not derealization, hallucination, or fugue. They normalize it as a peritraumatic response and screen for evolving PTSD without overcalling psychosis. Bottom line: An out-of-body view of oneself during trauma is depersonalization.

stem: A 13-year-old with a history of intellectual disability and infantile seizures is evaluated for a new skin finding on the lower back. On exam, there is a raised, thickened rough patch of skin approximately 5 cm in length. This cutaneous finding is most commonly associated with:
explanation_text: Intellectual disability, infantile spasms/seizures, and a thickened lumbosacral plaque (shagreen patch) are tuberous sclerosis. Port-wine stain = Sturge–Weber; café-au-lait/neurofibromas = NF1; vestibular schwannomas = NF2; hemangioblastomas = VHL. Teaching point: ID + early seizures + shagreen patch = TSC.
clinical_application: A 13-year-old with intellectual disability and a history of infantile spasms has a new thickened plaque on the lower back. The resident recognizes a shagreen patch and thinks tuberous sclerosis, not a port-wine Sturge–Weber stain or café-au-lait NF1. Dermatology and genetics join the team; they do not shrug it off as eczema. Bottom line: ID, early seizures, and a shagreen patch point to tuberous sclerosis.

Teaching point: New psychosis + butterfly rash → steroids for lupus cerebritis.

stem: Which disorder is most specifically associated with proactive aggression, as opposed to reactive aggression?

stem: An 11-year-old child who has previously been reluctant to take part in team sports asks a parent about joining the cross-country team at school. The parent responds that participating in team sports is an important experience to consider and asks whether the child would enjoy being on the team. This interaction is most congruent with which parenting style?
explanation_text: Warmth plus an invitation to reason ('team sports matter — would you enjoy it?') is authoritative parenting. Authoritarian would decree; permissive would shrug; uninvolved would not engage; 'demanding' is a dimension, not a style. Teaching point: Warm + firm + discussion = authoritative.
clinical_application: An 11-year-old who has avoided teams asks about cross-country. The parent says sports matter and asks whether the child would enjoy it. The resident hears warmth plus reasoning — authoritative parenting — not a decree and not a shrug. They reinforce the style rather than prescribing a sport. Bottom line: Warm, firm, and discussing it is authoritative parenting.

stem: A severely malnourished adolescent with anorexia nervosa is admitted to the hospital and started on a refeeding regimen. During the first weeks of refeeding, it is essential to closely monitor which of the following levels to avoid lethal complications?

stem: An adolescent went to the emergency department (ED) due to incredible restlessness and irritability after starting aripiprazole. A physician at the ED started the patient on a new medication, and the patient notes that symptoms of asthma have worsened. Which of the following medications was most likely prescribed by the ED physician?
explanation_text: Aripiprazole akathisia is treated with propranolol, which also can worsen asthma via beta-blockade. Anticholinergics (benztropine, diphenhydramine) treat dystonia better than akathisia. Dantrolene is for NMS. Mirtazapine is not the ED's first move. Teaching point: Akathisia + new wheeze = someone gave propranolol.
clinical_application: A teen started aripiprazole, then paced the ED in misery. Someone gave a pill; now their asthma is worse. The resident recognizes propranolol for akathisia — and its beta-blockade in the lungs. They switch the akathisia plan and treat the wheeze; benztropine would have been the wrong first guess. Bottom line: Akathisia plus new wheeze usually means someone gave propranolol.

stem: A physically healthy preschool child presents for evaluation of irritability and temper tantrums only around bedtime. For most nights over the past year, the child sat in bed tossing and turning at bedtime and repeatedly left the bedroom. Despite now sleeping with parents, the child continues to have frequent awakenings, along with delays in getting to sleep and early morning awakenings. The child has no other psychiatric or medical symptoms and no major environmental changes have occurred. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_text: A year of bedtime stalling, sleep-onset delay, night wakings, and early waking, confined to sleep and without medical/psychiatric competitors, is insomnia disorder. ODD would show daytime defiance. OSA/PLMD need snoring or kicks. ADHD is a daytime attention syndrome. Teaching point: Isolated chronic bedtime battle = pediatric insomnia, not ODD.
clinical_application: A physically well preschooler has a year of bedtime stalling, night wakings, and early rising, only around sleep. Daytime behavior is fine. The resident diagnoses insomnia disorder, not ODD or ADHD. The plan is a consistent bedtime routine and a return-to-bed protocol, not a stimulant trial. Bottom line: Isolated chronic bedtime battles are pediatric insomnia, not oppositionality.

stem: The mother of a six-month old is referred to Child Protective Services (CPS) after testing positive for methamphetamine during pregnancy. She tested positive recently for the same drug, resulting in a court judgment requiring that the child be taken into CPS care due to neglect. Which of the following principles does this case best exemplify?

Teaching point: CPS removal for neglect = parens patriae.
clinical_application: CPS takes custody of a 6-month-old after the mother tests positive for methamphetamine again. The resident names parens patriae — the state acting as parent — not police power or courtroom privilege. The note explains the legal frame to the team without editorializing about the mother. Bottom line: CPS removal for neglect is parens patriae.

stem: Which of the following factors threatens the external validity of study results?

options.text: Changes occurring in subjects over time
Characteristic differences between the sample and the target population
Unanticipated external events that change the conditions of the study

answer_text: Changes occurring in subjects over time
answer_raw: C. Changes occurring in subjects over time
explanation_text: External validity is generalizability. Time-related change in subjects can make findings fail to hold outside the study window. Repeat testing, regression to the mean, and history are classic internal-validity threats; sample-vs-population mismatch is the other major external-validity threat, but the keyed factor here is subject change over time. Teaching point: External validity asks 'will this still be true elsewhere/later?'
clinical_application: A fellow claims their school-based anxiety study will generalize everywhere. The resident asks what threatens external validity — including whether subjects change over the study window so the finding will not hold later. They separate that from internal-validity threats like testing and regression to the mean. Bottom line: External validity asks whether the result will still be true elsewhere and later.

stem: An adolescent diagnosed with social anxiety disorder presents to a clinic for a follow-up appointment. Which of the following statements by the patient is most concerning as a risk factor for suicide?

options.text: "I'm afraid I will stutter during my presentation."
"I'll never be able to get into my top choice college."
"I should have worn a cuter costume for the Halloween party."
"I wish I were not too afraid to go to a party for once and not spend weekends alone."
"I feel stupid because I said 'good morning' to someone even though it was the afternoon."

answer_text: "I wish I were not too afraid to go to a party for once and not spend weekends alone."
answer_raw: D. "I wish I were not too afraid to go to a party for once and not spend weekends alone."
explanation_text: Among social-anxiety cognitions, the one that flags suicide risk is painful isolation — wishing not to spend weekends alone. Fear of stuttering, costume regret, and post-hoc embarrassment are typical SAD thoughts; even catastrophic college worry is less specifically tied to suicide than loneliness/thwarted belonging. Teaching point: In SAD, loneliness/isolation is the suicide red flag.
clinical_application: A socially anxious teen says they wish they were not too afraid to go to a party and spend every weekend alone. Among the usual SAD cognitions, the resident hears loneliness as the suicide flag and does a careful safety assessment. Fear of stuttering or a costume regret would not have triggered the same urgency. Bottom line: In social anxiety, isolation is the suicide red flag.

stem: A child choked after eating. Since this episode, they hyperventilate, shake, and worry about dying when eating. The therapist first creates strategies to help them relax and then creates a graduated list of increasingly solid food for the child to try. This therapeutic intervention is using which of the following behavioral strategies?
explanation_text: Relaxation plus graded exposure to the feared food pairs a incompatible calm response with the CS — counterconditioning (systematic desensitization). Shaping reinforces successive approximations without the incompatible response; modeling is watching someone else; extinction is exposure without the CR being replaced; reinforcement is consequence-based. Teaching point: Relax + hierarchy = counterconditioning.
clinical_application: A child who choked now panics at any solid food. The therapist teaches relaxation, then builds a hierarchy from puree toward toast. The resident names counterconditioning — pairing calm with the old fear cue — not shaping or extinction alone. Parents stop force-feeding and follow the hierarchy. Bottom line: Relaxation plus a food hierarchy is counterconditioning.

stem: A 12-year-old child is in treatment for depression and ongoing interpersonal conflict with parents who have recently filed for divorce. The psychiatrist receives a subpoena to appear in court regarding the parents' custody dispute. Which term best describes the legal issue most relevant to the child's concern?
explanation_text: The child's fear that session content will be revealed in custody court is about privilege — the legal right to keep treatment communications out of evidence. Duty is the clinician's obligation, competence is capacity, autonomy is self-rule, parens patriae is the state's parenting power. Teaching point: 'Will the judge hear what I said?' = privilege.
clinical_application: A 12-year-old in the middle of a custody fight whispers, 'Will the judge hear what I say in here?' The resident names privilege — the legal shield on treatment communications — and explains its limits honestly. Duty, competence, and parens patriae are different problems. Bottom line: 'Will court hear my session?' is a privilege question.

stem: During psychodynamic play therapy, a child assigns the therapist to act as the child and themselves as the adult. Which of the following terms best describes this role reversal?

stem: The psychiatrist is consulted to evaluate a child who survived a house fire and has been in the ICU for two weeks to treat inhalation injuries. The resident diagnoses acute stress disorder, not delirium (attention would fluctuate) and not PTSD (too soon). A recent white blood cell count (WBC) is 6,100/mm3 and absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is 1,800/mm3. The following WBC is 3,800/mm3, and ANC is 1,100/mm3. Compared to an adult, which side effect of clozapine is this patient more likely to experience?
explanation_text: Relative to adults, youth on clozapine are keyed here as more likely to get akathisia (the vignette's falling ANC is a separate monitoring fact). Sialorrhea, weight, constipation, and hypotension occur in both ages; the exam's contrast is akathisia. Teaching point: Watch restlessness as well as ANC on pediatric clozapine.
clinical_application: An adolescent on clozapine has a falling ANC and also cannot sit still. The resident treats youth as more likely than adults to show akathisia on clozapine and still follows the neutropenia algorithm. They do not ignore the restlessness as 'just anxiety.' Bottom line: This exam keys akathisia as the clozapine side effect more likely in youth than adults.

stem: A child psychiatrist is working as a psychiatric consultant to a pediatric clinic using the collaborative care model. The child psychiatrist meets with the behavioral health care manager weekly to review their caseload. Together, they identify a 15-year-old with major depressive disorder whose PHQ-9 remains elevated despite taking fluoxetine 20mg prescribed by the pediatrician and engaging in weekly cognitive-behavioral therapy with the care manager. Which step should the psychiatric consultant recommend first?

options.text: Explore with the patient potential reasons for lack of improvement.
Cross-taper to a different selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor.
Provide family education and problem solving.
Refer to an intensive outpatient program.

answer_text: Explore with the patient potential reasons for lack of improvement.
answer_raw: A. Explore with the patient potential reasons for lack of improvement.
explanation_text: Collaborative-care consultant's first move when PHQ-9 is stuck on fluoxetine 20 + weekly CBT is to ask why (adherence, dose, residual stressors) — not immediately augment, switch, IOP, or extra family education. Teaching point: Treat-to-target starts with 'why isn't this working?'
clinical_application: Collaborative care: PHQ-9 still high on fluoxetine 20 mg plus weekly CBT. The consultant's first recommendation is to find out why — missed doses, residual trauma, wrong target. Not add bupropion and not jump to IOP. Bottom line: When collaborative-care numbers are stuck, explore why before switching.

stem: A child psychiatrist is working as a psychiatric consultant to a pediatric clinic using the collaborative care model. The child psychiatrist meets with the behavioral health care manager weekly to review their caseload. Together, they identify a 15-year-old with major depressive disorder whose PHQ-9 remains elevated despite taking fluoxetine 20mg prescribed by the pediatrician and engaging in weekly cognitive-behavioral therapy with the care manager. By reviewing the caseload and identifying patients who are not improving, the psychiatrist is following which of the following principles of collaborative care?
explanation_text: Reviewing the whole caseload to find who is not improving is population-based care. Accountability, EBM, patient-centeredness, and measurement-based treat-to-target are other collaborative-care principles (MBC is the PHQ-9 itself). Teaching point: Caseload registry review = population-based care.
clinical_application: The same consultant scans the whole registry for kids whose PHQ-9 is not moving. That is population-based care, not just good manners toward one patient. The measurement itself is treat-to-target. Bottom line: Caseload review to find who is not improving is population-based care.

stem: A ten-year-old-girl is brought to a psychiatrist's office by her mother for evaluation of temper outbursts, mood lability, daytime somnolence, and a compulsive need to put her toys in a certain order. Her mother reports that she struggles in school and has been diagnosed with learning disabilities. Her BMI places her in the obese category, and her height is below the normal range for her age. During the interview, the psychiatrist notices some areas of raw skin on the child's arm, and her mother reports that she picks at bug bites when she is stressed. Which of the following tests is most appropriate to order for the patient?
explanation_text: Short, obese, hypersomnolent, skin-picking, learning problems, and compulsive ordering is Prader–Willi; daytime somnolence plus obesity → order PSG for OSA (not EEG/EMG/MRI/MSLT first). Teaching point: PWS with sleepiness → sleep study.
clinical_application: A short, obese 10-year-old with rages, sleepiness, learning problems, ordering rituals, and skin picking. Before an MRI, the resident orders PSG: this is Prader–Willi until proven otherwise, and OSA is the sleep story. Genetics will confirm. Bottom line: PWS with hypersomnolence → polysomnography.

stem: A ten-year-old-girl is brought to a psychiatrist's office by her mother for evaluation of temper outbursts, mood lability, daytime somnolence, and a compulsive need to put her toys in a certain order. Her mother reports that she struggles in school and has been diagnosed with learning disabilities. Her BMI places her in the obese category, and her height is below the normal range for her age. During the interview, the psychiatrist notices some areas of raw skin on the child's arm, and her mother reports that she picks at bug bites when she is stressed. Which of the following is the inheritance pattern of the child's most likely genetic condition?
explanation_text: Prader–Willi is loss of paternal 15q11–13 (paternal deletion or maternal uniparental disomy 15). The keyed inheritance pattern is maternal disomy of chromosome 15. Not AD, triplet repeat, XR, or 22q. Teaching point: PWS genetics to remember = maternal UPD 15 (or paternal 15q deletion).
clinical_application: Same child. Parents ask how you 'get' Prader–Willi. The resident says maternal uniparental disomy 15 — or a paternal 15q deletion; the exam keys maternal disomy. Not 22q, not a triplet repeat. Bottom line: PWS inheritance they want = maternal disomy of chromosome 15.

stem: A 16-year-old is admitted to the hospital after a suicide attempt and symptoms consistent with severe major depressive disorder. Fluoxetine is started. options.text: Send hospital records to the school nurse.
Immediately begin evaluation for special education needs.

explanation_text: School connectedness is a daily in-school person who checks in — not sending records, rushing an IEP, assigning a school therapist, or starting CBITS (this was not a trauma admission). Teaching point: Connectedness = one named adult at school every day.

stem: A 16-year-old is admitted to the hospital after a suicide attempt and symptoms consistent with severe major depressive disorder. Fluoxetine is started. The hospital treatment team recommends therapy and school interventions. Which is the best rationale for selecting fluoxetine?

options.text: It is the least expensive antidepressant.
It has the smallest risk of adverse effects.
It is an FDA-approved medication for this age group.
It has the strongest evidence to support its use.
It has been shown to be the most efficacious in head-to-head trials.

answer_text: It has the strongest evidence to support its use.
answer_raw: D. It has the strongest evidence to support its use.
explanation_text: Fluoxetine is chosen because it has the strongest pediatric MDD evidence (TADS and others), not because it is cheapest, safest, or uniquely FDA-approved (escitalopram is also approved) or because head-to-head trials prove it most efficacious. Teaching point: Kid MDD SSRI with the best evidence = fluoxetine.
clinical_application: The team starts fluoxetine. The resident's reason is the evidence base — TADS and after — not price and not 'the only FDA-approved SSRI.' Escitalopram is approved too. Safety planning still sits beside the prescription. Bottom line: Fluoxetine is first because the pediatric MDD data are strongest.

stem: Which of the following symptoms commonly constitutes an aura experienced by a child with complex partial epilepsy? (Select three.)
answer_text: Jamais vu / Overwhelming fear / Olfactory hallucination
explanation_text: Complex-partial (focal impaired-awareness) auras include jamais vu, overwhelming fear, and olfactory hallucination. Lip smacking, circling, gelastic bursts, drowsiness, and LOC are ictal/post-ictal phenomena, not auras. Teaching point: Aura = psychic/sensory warning; automatisms are the seizure.
clinical_application: A child describes a funny smell, a wave of terror, and the world looking unfamiliar, then smacks her lips. The resident counts the first three as auras of a focal seizure; the lip smacking is ictal. EEG and MRI follow. Bottom line: Focal-seizure auras include jamais vu, fear, and olfactory hallucination — not automatisms.

stem: The core dimensional impairments of borderline personality disorders for adolescents, as described by the Alternative DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders, includes which of the following? (Select three.)
answer_text: Social dysfunction / Impairments in identity / Affective dysregulation
explanation_text: AMPD criterion A for adolescent borderline-range personality is impairment in identity, interpersonal functioning (social dysfunction), and affective dysregulation. Self-injury, anxiety, rigidity, psychosis, and somatic preoccupation are associated, not the three core dimensions. Teaching point: AMPD borderline core = identity + interpersonal + affect.
clinical_application: An adolescent looks borderline. Using AMPD, the resident checks identity, interpersonal function, and affective dysregulation. Cutting is associated, not one of the three core dimensions. They still treat the self-injury. Bottom line: AMPD borderline core = identity, social dysfunction, affective dysregulation.

stem: A psychiatrist orders pharmacogenetic testing for an adolescent patient, which reveals that the adolescent is a poor metabolizer of CYP2D6. Metabolism of which of the following antipsychotics would be most affected? (Select three.)
explanation_text: CYP2D6 poor metabolizers accumulate risperidone, aripiprazole, and perphenazine. Lurasidone/quetiapine/olanzapine/haloperidol/clozapine use other primary pathways (3A4, 1A2, etc.). Teaching point: 2D6 PM → go easy on risperidone, aripiprazole, perphenazine.
clinical_application: Pharmacogenetics: CYP2D6 poor metabolizer. The resident cuts expected doses of risperidone, aripiprazole, and perphenazine. Less worried about quetiapine or lurasidone on that pathway. Bottom line: 2D6 PM accumulates risperidone, perphenazine, and aripiprazole.

stem: Which of the following are mechanisms for epigenetic alterations in gene expression? (Select three.)
answer_text: DNA methylation / Histone modification / Posttranslational regulation by noncoding RNA
explanation_text: Epigenetic mechanisms: DNA methylation, histone modification, and noncoding-RNA post-transcriptional regulation. Chromatin elongation, inversions/translocations, DNase cleavage, and nucleotide substitution are not epigenetic regulation. Teaching point: Epigenetics = methylate, histone-mark, or microRNA — not a mutation.
clinical_application: A lecture asks for epigenetic mechanisms. The resident lists DNA methylation, histone marks, and noncoding RNA. Not a translocation or a base substitution — those change the sequence. Bottom line: Epigenetics = methylation, histone modification, noncoding RNA.

stem: Which of the following clinical features are consistent with benign Rolandic epilepsy? (Select three.)

options.text: Often accompanied by loss of consciousness

answer_text: Resolve by puberty / Usually occur at night / May cause lasting cognitive problems
explanation_text: Benign Rolandic (centrotemporal) epilepsy: nocturnal seizures, remits by puberty, and can leave cognitive problems despite the 'benign' name. It is not hippocampal, not typically before age 3, often needs no meds, does not cause permanent behavioral disease, and usually has no LOC. Teaching point: BRE = night seizures that grow out by puberty, not always cognitively silent.
clinical_application: Night facial twitches in a 9-year-old, EEG centrotemporal, otherwise well. The resident diagnoses benign Rolandic epilepsy: nocturnal, outgrown by puberty, and still warns that cognition can take a hit. They often hold meds. Bottom line: BRE is nocturnal and remits by puberty, but it is not always cognitively silent.

stem: Which of the following cortical areas make up the salience network responsible for responding to incoming cognitive, emotional, and homeostatic information? (Select three.)
explanation_text: The salience network that tags incoming cognitive/emotional/homeostatic signals is keyed as insula, anterior cingulate, and ventromedial prefrontal cortex. Medial PFC/PPC and PCC are more default-mode; DLPFC and lateral PPC more executive. Teaching point: Salience = insula + ACC (+ vmPFC on this exam).
clinical_application: A neuroscience slide on the salience network. The resident circles insula, anterior cingulate, and ventromedial PFC as the exam's three. Not the default-mode midline parietal nodes. Bottom line: Salience network on this exam = insula, ACC, vmPFC.

stem: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act allows for the disclosure of protected health information without first obtaining an individual's consent or authorization in which of the following situations? (Select three.)

options.text: A psychiatrist calls the patient's pediatrician to consult on abnormal lab values.
An outpatient psychiatrist calls a patient's nanny to gather collateral information.
An inpatient psychiatric unit faxes a discharge summary to the outpatient psychiatrist.
An outpatient psychiatrist calls a school to discuss a patient's academic performance.
An emergency room psychiatrist faxes a discharge summary to the patient's school.
A psychiatrist on an inpatient unit answers questions from the patient's adult sibling over the phone.
An outpatient psychiatrist calls an outpatient therapist at another organization to coordinate care of a shared patient.
An outpatient psychiatrist calls the psychiatrist of the patient's parent to discuss concerns brought up by the patient during a session.

answer_text: A psychiatrist calls the patient's pediatrician to consult on abnormal lab values. / An inpatient psychiatric unit faxes a discharge summary to the outpatient psychiatrist. / An outpatient psychiatrist calls an outpatient therapist at another organization to coordinate care of a shared patient.
explanation_text: HIPAA TPO allows treatment communications without extra authorization: consult the pediatrician, send a d/c summary to the outpatient psychiatrist, coordinate with the patient's other therapist. Nanny, school, sibling, and the parent's psychiatrist are not TPO. Teaching point: TPO = treaters of this patient, not the school or the family.
clinical_application: Someone wants to call the nanny and the school without a release. The resident says HIPAA TPO covers the pediatrician, the outpatient psychiatrist getting the d/c summary, and the other treating therapist. Not the nanny, school, sibling, or parent's doctor. Bottom line: TPO is this patient's treaters, not collateral civilians.

stem: Which of the following genetic disorders are X-linked recessive? (Select three.)
answer_text: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome / Rett syndrome / Fragile X syndrome
explanation_text: The exam keys Lesch–Nyhan, Rett, and Fragile X as the X-linked set. Lesch–Nyhan (HPRT) is the classic X-linked recessive; Rett (MECP2) and Fragile X (FMR1) are X-linked (Rett typically dominant/male-lethal; Fragile X is X-linked with unusual penetrance). Gaucher, PKU, and AT are autosomal recessive. Angelman/PWS are 15q imprinting. Teaching point: X-linked trio they want = Lesch–Nyhan, Rett, Fragile X.
clinical_application: Genetics pimp session: name the X-linked set. The resident gives Lesch–Nyhan, Rett, and Fragile X — the keyed three. Gaucher and PKU stay autosomal recessive; they still know Rett is classically X-linked dominant. Bottom line: The X-linked trio this item wants is Lesch–Nyhan, Rett, and Fragile X.

stem: An adolescent has been brought into the emergency department after fainting during a wrestling match.
